newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-EDDERY CONFIRMS 11TH JOCKEYS' TITLE.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-EDDERY CONFIRMS 11TH JOCKEYS' TITLE.

text.p: British horse racing's clash of the generations ended with honours roughly even as the Flat season on turf came to a quiet close at Folkestone on Monday.
Pat Eddery, 44, struck a blow for the establishment by winning the jockeys' championship for the 11th time.
His total of 186 winners was the third-best tally of his career and gave him the title by 37 from Richard Quinn.

But the Irishman will know that fortune smiled on him as the 20-year younger Frankie Dettori had his defence of the championship title bid wrecked by injury and suspension yet still ended up only 63 winners off the top of the table.
And Dettori's feat at Ascot in September is sure to be the most remembered of all in 1996.

He became the first jockey ever to ride all seven winners on a card, an historic achievement which put him in the running to be BBC sports personality of the year and even led to his presenting a television pop programme last week.

Eddery's prospects for 1997 are less certain. Young pretender Kieren Fallon, third in the table this year with 136 victories, takes over as stable-jockey to Henry Cecil, who supplied 54 of Eddery's winners.
Cecil himself lost his season-long battle to take the trainers' championship for a 10th time.
That crown went by around $60,000 to Godolphin's trainer Saeed bin Suroor, a 30-year-old former Dubai policeman who clinched the prize just 18 months after his arrival in this country.
The most notable figures missing when the turf action resumes next spring will be multiple Group One-winning trainers Guy Harwood and Tom Jones who both announced their retirements during the season.
But the racing world has its fingers crossed that Willie Carson's name will be back on the jockeys' board at the curtain-raising meeting at Doncaster on March 20.

The 54-year-old Scot is recovering from serious injuries suffered when he was kicked in the paddock by his intended mount at Newbury and will be spurred on by the prospect of riding 2000 Guineas winter favourite Bahhare in 1997.
And he will be heartened by the example of Walter Swinburn whose life was in danger after a fall in Hong Kong in February.

He won on his first comeback ride at Windsor in August and went on to gain one of the most valuable successes of his career when Pilsudksi beat Singspiel to give Michael Stoute a one-two in the Breeders' Cup Turf a Woodbine in Canada.
